description: Determines whether an intermediate product or assembled structure qualifies as an 'excisable good' by evaluating if it is practically capable of being brought to the market and sold.
application_scenario: Use when the revenue attempts to levy excise duty on intermediate chemicals, captively consumed goods, or site-assembled machinery that are neither sold nor practically marketable in their existing form.
reasoning_flow: Identify the specific intermediate product, captively consumed item, or assembled plant on which the revenue seeks to levy excise duty.
Apply the dual test of excisability: first, that a distinct new article has emerged through manufacture, and second, that it satisfies the 'marketability test'.
Examine the physical and commercial realities of the item at the intermediate stage, assessing factors such as chemical stability, commercial purity, packaging, or permanent embedment to the earth.
Require the revenue to discharge the burden of proving that the item is known to the market and practically capable of being bought and sold.
Quash the duty demand if the item fails the marketability test, ruling that mere mention in the tariff schedule does not automatically render an unmarketable intermediate product an excisable good.
example_application: A manufacturer produces a crude chemical compound that is immediately consumed through a continuous pipe to make a final product. The court finds the intermediate compound lacks commercial purity and cannot be transported or sold, thus holding it non-excisable for failing the marketability test.
shared_pattern: The revenue attempts to tax an intermediate or embedded item; the court rejects the levy because the item fails the practical test of marketability.
scope_exclusions: Do not use for classifying goods that are admittedly sold in the open market, or for interpreting the rate of duty applicable to a recognized commercial product.

description: Determines the true assessable value of manufactured goods for excise levy by capturing the actual wholesale price, adding buyer-supplied material costs, and excluding post-manufacturing values or statutory duties.
application_scenario: Use when there is a dispute over the correct valuation base for excise duty, such as when buyers provide free materials, when the value of a buyer's trademark is involved, or when the gross sale price must be treated as a cum-duty price.
reasoning_flow: Identify the baseline wholesale transaction price or contract price at which the manufacturer clears the goods at the factory gate.
Determine whether this price constitutes the sole consideration for the sale, or if there are embedded or ancillary considerations.
Add the intrinsic value of any direct manufacturing inputs supplied free of cost by the buyer (e.g., containers) to the base price to reflect the true manufacturing cost.
Exclude elements that do not contribute to the intrinsic manufacturing value (such as the value of the buyer's trademark) and statutory levies (treating the gross price as a cum-duty price).
Compute the final assessable value that strictly reflects the intrinsic wholesale manufacturing value, ensuring the tax base is neither artificially depressed nor improperly inflated.
example_application: A manufacturer sells batteries at a contracted price but receives free containers from the buyer. The court rules that the assessable value must include the cost of the free containers as they are integral to the finished good, but excludes the excise duty element by treating the final gross realization as a cum-duty price.
shared_pattern: The court reconstructs the commercial transaction price to isolate the true intrinsic manufacturing value, adding hidden material costs while stripping out subsequent duties or external brand values.
scope_exclusions: Do not use for customs valuation of imported goods, determining dumping margins, or computing loss of dependency in tort claims.
